drills.q: State the one question each of the four gates (POC, Prototype, MVP, Production) answers.
drills.a: POC: can it be built at all? Prototype: is it the right thing to build? MVP: will real users adopt it at small scale? Production: will it hold up under real load/failure/cost/ops indefinitely?

drills.q: Your team wants to ship POC code to production because it 'already works' and there's a deadline. What's wrong with this reasoning?
drills.a: POC code was deliberately built to skip every production concern (scale, failure handling, security, observability, cost, ownership) to answer one narrow technical question on a small sample. 'It works' is true only for that narrow case; production will discover the gaps live, more expensively than a design review would have.

drills.q: What does RAND's 33.8%-abandoned-before-production figure specifically tell you about how pilots are being run?
drills.a: It means a third of AI project failures are exactly the kind the POC/prototype gates exist to catch cheaply — their still happening at that scale suggests those early gates are being skipped or run without real (measured, user-behavior-based) exit criteria, not that the gates don't work.

drills.q: A prototype tested well with 8 target users but the MVP saw zero adoption. What's the likely explanation?
drills.a: The prototype likely used a Wizard-of-Oz element (a human silently handling the hard part) or a small curated sample that doesn't represent the MVP's real launch cohort — a positive prototype signal validates the interaction concept, not the real system's ability to deliver it.

drills.q: What's the AI-specific gate addition that a traditional CRUD feature's MVP-to-production path doesn't need, and why?
drills.a: An automated golden-set evaluation harness gating every model/prompt/retrieval-config change, plus production drift monitoring — because generative output quality can silently degrade in ways a binary pass/fail test suite (built for deterministic code) wouldn't catch.

drills.q: Someone argues MVP and production are the same code, just 'more polished.' Counter this.
drills.a: The difference is which risk category is retired, not degree of polish — MVP retires market/adoption risk with informal ops; production retires operational/scale risk (resilience patterns, on-call ownership, tested rollback, capacity planning). An MVP can be bug-free on its happy path and still fail production readiness because the failure-mode handling was never built.

drills.q: Design exit criteria for the MVP gate of a new AI search feature.
drills.a: Real usage/retention numbers from a real (if small) pilot cohort over a real time window, e.g. '60% weekly-active among 50 pilot users after 4 weeks, unit cost per query under $X' — plus a golden-set eval harness already gating changes before this gate closes.

drills.q: Leadership wants to skip the prototype stage entirely for a new AI feature to 'move fast.' How do you respond?
drills.a: Separate compressing time (legitimate — a prototype can be days) from skipping the question (risky — betting the MVP investment on an unvalidated assumption). If the product/UX risk is genuinely low (internal tool, well-understood need), skipping is defensible; for a genuinely novel external-facing interaction, name the RAND-documented risk explicitly rather than silently complying or resisting.

drills.q: An MVP pilot cohort loved a feature, but full production rollout showed much lower engagement. What gate-design flaw does this expose?
drills.a: The pilot cohort was likely self-selected and non-representative (early adopters, more tolerant users) — MVP exit criteria measured on it can pass while masking a mismatch with the general population, arguing pilot-cohort selection should itself be a deliberate, examined choice.

drills.q: You have zero time for either hardening work or an explicit risk-acceptance conversation before a forced production deadline. What do you do?
drills.a: Say plainly that you don't have time to ship safely rather than let the deadline silently absorb the risk. Name the specific untested failure modes and cost/scale assumptions so leadership has an informed choice, even under time pressure — this converts a silent risk inheritance into an explicit, accountable decision.
